s: Which one of the following is included within the scope of a Money Bill under Article 110(1) of the Constitution?
o: Fees for licences issued by local authorities
Taxes imposed by a municipality for local purposes
Imposition of fines by a criminal court
Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax
x: A Money Bill may deal with the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of a tax. Fines, licence fees and local taxes are not, by themselves, matters of a Money Bill.
tq: Identify the exact constitutional subject instead of selecting nearby revenue-related terms.
sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following is NOT a matter specified in Article 110(1) as relating to a Money Bill?
o: Appropriation of money out of the Consolidated Fund of India
Borrowing of money by the Government of India
Custody of the Consolidated Fund of India or the Contingency Fund of India
Regulation of fees for services rendered by a local authority
x: Article 110(1) covers borrowing, custody and appropriation of specified public funds, among other matters. Regulation of fees for local-authority services is not a Money Bill matter.
tq: Find the option that falls outside the specifically enumerated constitutional subjects.
sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding a Money Bill:
1. It may deal with the custody of money in the Public Account of India.
2. It may provide for the receipt of money into, or the audit of, the Consolidated Fund of India.
3. It may deal with matters incidental to the matters specified in Article 110(1).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: All three statements describe matters covered by Article 110(1), including Public Account custody, receipt or audit of Consolidated Fund money, and incidental matters.
tq: Check each statement against the constitutional list and use the comprehensive option only when every item fits.
sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

s: A Bill containing provisions exclusively relating to the matters specified in Article 110(1) can be introduced in Parliament only when which one of the following conditions is satisfied?
o: It is introduced in the Lok Sabha by a private member after prior approval of the Rajya Sabha
It is introduced in the Lok Sabha by a minister on the recommendation of the President
It is introduced in either House by any member with the consent of the Speaker
It is introduced in the Rajya Sabha by a minister on the recommendation of the President
x: A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, only by a minister, and only on the President's recommendation.
tq: Split the conditions by asking who introduces, where it is introduced and whose recommendation is required.
sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

s: Who certifies that a Bill is a Money Bill?
o: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
The Union Finance Minister
The President of India
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
x: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill. The Speaker's decision is treated as final under Article 110(3).
tq: Use the constitutional office specifically entrusted with the certification power.
sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

s:
With reference to the Speaker's certificate on a Money Bill, consider the following statements:
1. The decision of the Speaker under Article 110(3) is final.
2. The certificate is endorsed on the Bill when it is sent to the Rajya Sabha.
3. The certificate is also endorsed when the Bill is presented to the President.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: The Speaker's decision is final under Article 110(3), and the certificate is endorsed on the Bill sent to the Rajya Sabha and presented to the President.
tq: Track the certificate through both constitutional transmission stages rather than limiting it to introduction.
sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

s: If the Rajya Sabha does not return a Money Bill within the prescribed period, the Bill is:
o: Deemed to have been passed by both Houses in the form passed by the Lok Sabha
Returned to the President for reconsideration
Referred to a joint sitting
Rejected by Parliament
x: When the Rajya Sabha does not return a Money Bill within 14 days, it is deemed to have been passed by both Houses in the form passed by the Lok Sabha.
tq: Apply the consequence of non-return instead of treating silence as rejection or deadlock.
sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the role of the Rajya Sabha in relation to a Money Bill?
o: It must pass the Bill without any recommendation within fourteen days.
It may return the Bill with recommendations, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject.
It may reject the Bill by a simple majority and thereby terminate it.
It may amend the Bill and its amendments are binding on the Lok Sabha.
x: The Rajya Sabha can make recommendations and return the Bill within 14 days, but the Lok Sabha may accept or reject those recommendations.
tq: Separate the recommendatory role of the Rajya Sabha from the binding amendment power applicable to ordinary Bills.
sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following statements regarding the President's action on a Money Bill is correct?
o: The President may assent to it or withhold assent, but cannot return it for reconsideration.
The President must refer it to the Supreme Court before giving assent.
The President may return it to Parliament for reconsideration once.
The President has no constitutional role after the Speaker certifies it.
x: Under Article 111, a Money Bill cannot be returned by the President for reconsideration. The President may assent to it or withhold assent; in practice, assent follows the prior recommendation for introduction.
tq: Test the important exception that distinguishes Money Bills from ordinary Bills at the assent stage.
sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

s: Which case upheld the Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill, while the Money-Bill issue was subsequently referred to a larger bench in another case?
o: K.S. Puttaswamy, 2018; Rojer Mathew, 2019
Rojer Mathew, 2018; K.S. Puttaswamy, 2019
K.S. Puttaswamy, 2019; Rojer Mathew, 2018
Justice K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017; Rojer Mathew, 2020
x: The Aadhaar Act was upheld as a Money Bill in K.S. Puttaswamy (2018). The Money-Bill question was later referred to a seven-judge bench in Rojer Mathew (2019).
tq: Anchor the judicial developments by matching the case names with their years and sequence.
sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

s: The reference in Rojer Mathew concerning the Money-Bill issue was made to a bench consisting of:
o: Nine judges
Seven judges
Five judges
Three judges
x: In Rojer Mathew (2019), the Money-Bill question was referred to a larger seven-judge bench.
tq: Retain the exact numerical composition of the larger bench rather than relying on the usual constitutional-bench size.
sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

s: A Government Bill in Parliament ordinarily requires what period of notice before introduction, whereas a Private Member's Bill requires what period?
o: 14 days and 1 month respectively
7 days and 1 month respectively
7 days and 14 days respectively
1 month and 7 days respectively
x: A Government Bill requires seven days' notice, while a Private Member's Bill requires one month's notice before introduction.
tq: Compare the two notice periods directly and watch for their reversal in the options.
sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the First Reading of an ordinary Bill?
o: Leave to introduce is sought, and the title and objectives are presented; it may then be published in the Gazette
The President decides whether to return the Bill for reconsideration
Clause-by-clause voting on amendments takes place
The Bill is accepted or rejected as a whole without substantive amendments
x: The First Reading concerns leave to introduce the Bill, its title and objectives, and publication in the Gazette. Clause-by-clause consideration belongs to the Second Reading, while assent is a later stage.
tq: Match the legislative action with the correct reading instead of confusing adjacent stages.
sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. First Reading — Publication in the Gazette
2. Second Reading — Committee stage and clause-by-clause consideration
3. Third Reading — Acceptance or rejection of the Bill as a whole
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: All three pairs are correctly matched. The Second Reading includes general discussion, committee consideration and clause-by-clause voting, while the Third Reading concerns the Bill as a whole.
tq: Use the stage-wise table structure to verify each pair independently.
sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

s: During which reading of an ordinary Bill does the committee stage occur?
o: Third Reading
Presidential Reading
First Reading
Second Reading
x: The committee stage forms part of the Second Reading, along with general discussion and consideration of the Bill clause by clause.
tq: Locate the committee stage within the sequence of readings rather than treating it as a separate reading.
sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

s:
Which of the following is characteristic of the Third Reading of an ordinary Bill?
1. The Bill is considered and voted upon as a whole.
2. Amendments of substance are ordinarily not made at this stage.
3. The Bill may be accepted or rejected as a whole.
Select the correct answer using the code below.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: The Third Reading deals with the Bill as a whole; it may be accepted or rejected, and substantive amendments are not made at this stage.
tq: Combine the defining features of one stage and reject options that omit a linked feature.
sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

s: After an ordinary Bill is passed by one House, the other House may:
o: Return it only to the President
Pass it, amend it, reject it, or keep it pending for six months
Certify it as a Money Bill
Only pass it without alteration
x: The second House may pass, amend or reject an ordinary Bill, or keep it pending for six months, potentially creating a deadlock.
tq: Choose the option that lists the complete range of legislative responses rather than an exclusive power.
sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

s: The absence of a constitutionally prescribed time limit for the President to act on an ordinary Bill makes possible what is commonly known as:
o: Suspensive dissolution
Pocket veto
Collective veto
Absolute veto only
x: Since no fixed time limit is prescribed for presidential action, the President may keep an ordinary Bill pending indefinitely, a situation known as a pocket veto.
tq: Link the procedural omission—the absence of a time limit—with its established constitutional term.
sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

s:
Arrange the following stages of an ordinary Bill in the correct chronological order:
A. Consideration by the second House
B. First Reading in the originating House
C. Presidential action
D. Second and Third Readings in the originating House
o: B, D, A, C
D, B, A, C
B, A, D, C
A, B, D, C
x: The Bill is first introduced in the originating House, undergoes its Second and Third Readings, is transmitted to the second House, and then reaches the President.
tq: Fix the first and final stages, then place the two parliamentary House stages between them.
sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

s: A deadlock arising because the two Houses finally disagree on amendments to an ordinary Bill is dealt with through the mechanism provided in:
o: Article 109
Article 110
Article 108
Article 111
x: Article 108 provides for a joint sitting to resolve specified deadlocks between the two Houses over an ordinary Bill.
tq: Match the deadlock mechanism with the correct constitutional article, distinguishing it from Articles 109–111.
sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

s:
Which of the following situations can constitute a deadlock warranting consideration of a joint sitting under Article 108?
1. The other House rejects the Bill.
2. The Houses finally disagree on amendments.
3. The other House does not pass the Bill for more than six months, excluding specified periods of prorogation or adjournment.
Select the correct answer using the code below.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: All three situations are grounds for a joint sitting. In calculating the six-month period, periods of prorogation and adjournment over four consecutive days are excluded.
tq: Test all three constitutional grounds together, including the qualifying exclusion in the time condition.
sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

s: For the purpose of the six-month period relevant to a joint sitting, which periods are excluded?
o: Periods of prorogation and periods of adjournment over four consecutive days
All periods of parliamentary recess without exception
Only periods of dissolution of the Lok Sabha
Only periods during which the President is absent from India
x: Periods of prorogation and periods of adjournment over four consecutive days are excluded while computing the relevant six-month period.
tq: Read the time rule precisely and avoid the extreme claim that every recess is excluded.
sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

s: If the President does not summon a joint sitting after a deadlock under Article 108, the Bill:
o: Automatically becomes law after six months
Is deemed to have been rejected by the Rajya Sabha only
Comes to an end
Must be referred to the Supreme Court
x: If the President does not summon the joint sitting, the Bill comes to an end. It does not automatically become law or receive judicial certification.
tq: Apply the consequence of non-summoning instead of assuming that a deadlocked Bill remains permanently pending.
sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

s: A decision at a joint sitting is taken by:
o: A unanimous vote of the presiding officers of both Houses
A simple majority of members present and voting in both Houses together
A special majority of the total membership of both Houses
A two-thirds majority of members present and voting in each House separately
x: The Bill is decided by a simple majority of the members of both Houses present and voting together at the joint sitting.
tq: Distinguish the voting threshold and the combined body voting from special-majority procedures.
sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following sets contains only the categories of Bills excluded from a joint sitting?
o: Appropriation Bills and Ordinary Bills
Private Members' Bills and Government Bills
Ordinary Bills and Financial Bills
Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills
x: Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills cannot be referred to a joint sitting. Financial Bills of types I and II can go to a joint sitting.
tq: Identify the two express exclusions and avoid treating every financial measure as excluded.
sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following statements regarding Financial Bills is correct?
o: Financial Bills of types I and II can be referred to a joint sitting.
A Financial Bill can be introduced only in the Rajya Sabha.
A Financial Bill is always treated exactly like a Money Bill in the Rajya Sabha.
Both types of Financial Bills are constitutionally excluded from a joint sitting.
x: Financial Bills of types I and II can go to a joint sitting. They must not be confused with Money Bills, which are excluded from the joint-sitting procedure.
tq: Separate Financial Bills from Money Bills by testing the consequence that differs between them.
sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with a joint sitting of Parliament?
1. 1961 — Dowry Prohibition Bill
2. 1978 — Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill
3. 2002 — Prevention of Terrorism Bill
Select the correct answer using the code below.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: All three pairs are correct. These are the three occasions on which a joint sitting of Parliament was held: 1961, 1978 and 2002 respectively.
tq: Verify each year–Bill pair independently, using the distinctive chronological list as the anchor.
sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

s: How many joint sittings of the Indian Parliament have been held for resolving legislative deadlocks, as represented by the recorded instances of 1961, 1978 and 2002?
o: Five
Four
Two
Three
x: Joint sittings have been held only three times: for the Dowry Prohibition Bill, the Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill and the Prevention of Terrorism Bill.
tq: Count the complete historical list rather than inferring frequency from the constitutional provision.
sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

s: A Bill passed by the Rajya Sabha is pending before the Lok Sabha when the Lok Sabha is dissolved. What is the position of the Bill?
o: It does not lapse
It becomes law after the dissolution
It lapses
It is automatically referred to a joint sitting
x: A Bill passed by the Rajya Sabha and pending in the Lok Sabha lapses when the Lok Sabha is dissolved.
tq: Apply the rule that a Bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses irrespective of which House passed it first.
sec: Lapsing of bills on dissolution of Lok Sabha

s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding a joint sitting and dissolution of the Lok Sabha?
o: A joint sitting can be summoned even after the Bill has lapsed
A joint sitting cannot be summoned for a Bill that has already lapsed
Every Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha is automatically sent to a joint sitting
A lapsed Bill must be placed before a joint sitting in the next session
x: A joint sitting cannot be summoned for a Bill that has already lapsed. Dissolution may terminate the Bill before the deadlock-resolution procedure can operate.
tq: Distinguish the existence of a Bill from the procedural stage required for a joint sitting.
sec: Lapsing of bills on dissolution of Lok Sabha

s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the effect of parliamentary proceedings:

List-I (Event)
a. Adjournment or adjournment sine die
b. Prorogation
c. Dissolution of the Lok Sabha

a. List-II (Effect)
i. All pending business before the Lok Sabha lapses
 ii. Pending notices generally lapse, except notices for introducing Bills
 iii. Bills do not lapse and may be taken up in the next session

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
o: a–iii, b–ii, c–i
a–ii, b–iii, c–i
a–iii, b–i, c–ii
a–i, b–ii, c–iii
x: Adjournment or adjournment sine die does not cause Bills to lapse; prorogation causes pending notices to lapse except notices for introducing Bills; dissolution causes all pending business before the Lok Sabha to lapse.
tq: Start from the sure pair that adjournment does not terminate Bills, then match prorogation and dissolution.
sec: Lapsing of bills on dissolution of Lok Sabha

s:
With reference to Financial Bill-I under Article 117(1), consider the following statements:
1. It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha.
2. It requires the President's recommendation at the stage of introduction.
3. The Rajya Sabha can only recommend amendments to it.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the Rajya Sabha may amend or reject a Financial Bill-I; its powers are not restricted to making recommendations.
tq: Trap the transfer of the Rajya Sabha's limited Money Bill power to Financial Bill-I.
sec: Money Bill vs Financial Bills (I, II) vs Finance Bill

s: Which one of the following correctly describes a Financial Bill-II under Article 117(3)?
o: It can be introduced in either House and requires the President's recommendation at the consideration stage
It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha by a Minister
It contains exclusively matters specified in Article 110
It cannot be amended or rejected by the Rajya Sabha
x: A Financial Bill-II may be introduced in either House, by a Minister or a private member, but the President's recommendation is required when it is taken into consideration. The Rajya Sabha may amend or reject it.
tq: Separate Financial Bill-II from both the Lok Sabha-only rule and the Money Bill rule.
sec: Money Bill vs Financial Bills (I, II) vs Finance Bill

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Financial Bill-II — Joint sitting permitted
Money Bill — Speaker's certificate required
Financial Bill-I — Speaker's certificate required
Money Bill — Joint sitting not permitted
x: A Financial Bill-I does not require the Speaker's certificate. A Money Bill requires that certificate; joint sitting is permitted for Financial Bills-I and II but not for a Money Bill.
tq: Check the certification column separately from the House of introduction and joint-sitting columns.
sec: Money Bill vs Financial Bills (I, II) vs Finance Bill

s:
Arrange the following Bills in the order of the extent of matters under Article 110 covered by them, beginning with the widest coverage:
A. Financial Bill-II
B. Money Bill
C. Financial Bill-I

Select the correct sequence.
o: B, C, A
C, B, A
B, A, C
A, C, B
x: A Money Bill deals exclusively with Article 110 matters; a Financial Bill-I contains such matters partly along with other matters; a Financial Bill-II contains none of the Article 110 matters.
tq: Order the Bills by comparing the extent of Article 110 content rather than their financial character alone.
sec: Money Bill vs Financial Bills (I, II) vs Finance Bill

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill.
2. Every Financial Bill is a Money Bill.
3. A Finance Bill gives effect to the tax proposals of the Budget.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because every financial bill is not a Money Bill; the categories are not identical.
tq: Watch for the reversed inclusion trap in the paired expressions 'every Money Bill' and 'every Financial Bill'.
sec: Money Bill vs Financial Bills (I, II) vs Finance Bill

s: Which one of the following statements regarding a Finance Bill is correct?
o: It is always introduced first in the Rajya Sabha
It can never be certified as a Money Bill
It gives effect to the tax proposals contained in the Budget
It cannot contain any proposal relating to taxation
x: A Finance Bill gives effect to the Budget's tax proposals and is usually certified as a Money Bill. It is not always introduced in the Rajya Sabha and may involve taxation proposals.
tq: Use the functional meaning of a Finance Bill instead of treating it as identical to every Financial Bill.
sec: Money Bill vs Financial Bills (I, II) vs Finance Bill

s: A proposed amendment to a Financial Bill-I seeks to abolish an existing tax. Is the President's recommendation required for such an amendment?
o: No, because Financial Bills-I never require recommendation
Yes, because every amendment to a tax requires recommendation
No, an amendment reducing or abolishing a tax does not require such recommendation
Yes, but only when the Bill is pending in the Rajya Sabha
x: An amendment reducing or abolishing a tax does not require the President's recommendation. An amendment increasing a tax requires such recommendation.
tq: Distinguish the direction of the tax change; reducing or abolishing tax is treated differently from increasing it.
sec: Money Bill vs Financial Bills (I, II) vs Finance Bill

s: Which one of the following statements correctly compares the President's power to return the Bills?
o: The President cannot return any financial legislation
The President can return only a Financial Bill-II
The President cannot return a Money Bill but can return Financial Bills-I and II
The President can return a Money Bill but cannot return either Financial Bill
x: A Money Bill cannot be returned by the President for reconsideration, whereas Financial Bills-I and II can be returned.
tq: Compare the President's return power across the three categories instead of assuming all financial Bills follow the Money Bill rule.
sec: Money Bill vs Financial Bills (I, II) vs Finance Bill

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 117(3) — Financial Bill-II at the consideration stage
Article 3 — Formation of new States or alteration of their areas, boundaries or names
Article 117(1) — Financial Bill-I
Article 274 — Bills relating exclusively to expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India
x: Article 274 concerns Bills affecting taxation in which States are interested. Bills involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India require recommendation under Article 117(3).
tq: Use the Article-subject match and reject the swapped Article 274 description.
sec: Bills by House of introduction; President's prior recommendation

s: A Bill involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India is proposed for consideration. At what stage is the President's recommendation required under Article 117(3)?
o: No recommendation is required at any stage
Before the Bill is taken into consideration
Only before its introduction in the Rajya Sabha
Only after the Bill has been passed by both Houses
x: For a Financial Bill-II involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India, the President's recommendation is required before the Bill is taken into consideration.
tq: Focus on the stage specified—consideration—not merely on the fact that the Bill concerns public expenditure.
sec: Bills by House of introduction; President's prior recommendation

s: Which one of the following statements regarding State legislation is correct?
o: Such a Bill can be introduced only in the Rajya Sabha
Such a Bill requires the Speaker's certificate as a Money Bill
A Bill restricting inter-State trade may be introduced in a State Legislature without any prior sanction
A Bill restricting inter-State trade requires the President's previous sanction before introduction in a State Legislature
x: A State Bill restricting inter-State trade cannot be introduced without the President's previous sanction.
tq: Apply the prior-sanction rule at the State level and distinguish it from parliamentary Money Bill certification.
sec: Bills by House of introduction; President's prior recommendation

s: Which of the following is the correct distinction between a Government Bill and a Private Member's Bill?
o: A Government Bill is introduced by a Minister, whereas a Private Member's Bill is introduced by an MP who is not a Minister
A Private Member's Bill can be introduced only in the Rajya Sabha
A Government Bill is introduced by any MP, whereas a Private Member's Bill is introduced only by a Minister
Both Bills are drafted exclusively by the Law Ministry
x: A Government Bill is introduced by a Minister. A Private Member's Bill is introduced by any Member of Parliament who is not a Minister.
tq: Discriminate the two Bills by the identity of the member introducing them.
sec: Private member's bills vs government bills

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Government Bill — one month's notice
Private Member's Bill — seven days' notice
Government Bill — rejection necessarily signals loss of confidence in the government
Private Member's Bill — defeat has no bearing on the government's continuation in office
x: Defeat of a Private Member's Bill does not affect the government's continuation in office. Government Bills generally require seven days' notice, while Private Members' Bills require one month's notice; rejection of a Government Bill may signal loss of confidence.
tq: Compare notice period and political consequence together to avoid swapping the two categories.
sec: Private member's bills vs government bills

s: A Member of Parliament who is not a Minister intends to introduce a Bill. Which of the following is applicable to the Bill?
o: It is a Financial Bill-I and must be introduced by a Minister
It is a Private Member's Bill and ordinarily requires one month's notice
It is a Government Bill and requires seven days' notice
It is a Money Bill and requires no recommendation
x: A Bill introduced by an MP who is not a Minister is a Private Member's Bill. Such a Bill ordinarily requires one month's notice.
tq: Identify the category from the status of the proposer, then apply the corresponding notice period.
sec: Private member's bills vs government bills

s: Who normally drafts a Government Bill and who drafts a Private Member's Bill?
o: The Government Bill is drafted by the Rajya Sabha Secretariat, while the Private Member's Bill is drafted by the President
The Government Bill is drafted by the department with the Law Ministry, while the Private Member's Bill is drafted by the member
Both are drafted by the concerned Member of Parliament
Both are drafted by the Election Commission
x: A Government Bill is drafted by the concerned department in association with the Law Ministry. A Private Member's Bill is drafted by the member introducing it.
tq: Use the drafting agency as the decisive distinction between Government and Private Member's Bills.
sec: Private member's bills vs government bills

s: Which one of the following statements about the Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions is correct?
o: It is a committee of the President's Secretariat
It is a committee of the Rajya Sabha that certifies Money Bills
It is a joint committee that drafts all Government Bills
It is a Lok Sabha committee that classifies Private Members' Bills and allots time to them
x: The Lok Sabha's Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions classifies such Bills and allots time for their discussion.
tq: Identify the correct House and function instead of confusing this committee with the Business Advisory Committee.
sec: Private member's bills vs government bills

s: Which one of the following functions is performed by the Lok Sabha's Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions?
o: It recommends the President's assent to Money Bills
It decides whether a Government Bill should be returned by the President
It appoints Ministers of the Union
It examines Private Members' constitutional amendment Bills before their introduction
x: The Lok Sabha committee examines constitutional amendment Bills introduced by Private Members before their introduction, besides classifying Bills and allotting time.
tq: Test the committee's specific procedural role rather than its general legislative association.
sec: Private member's bills vs government bills

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Private Members' Bills:
1. A Private Member's Bill is introduced by an MP who is not a Minister.
2. Its defeat necessarily amounts to a loss of confidence in the government.
3. In the Lok Sabha, time for such Bills is allotted by the Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false: defeat of a Private Member's Bill has no bearing on the government's continuation in office.
tq: Reject the political-consequence trap and retain the proposer and time-allocation statements.
sec: Private member's bills vs government bills

s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Rajya Sabha's procedure for Private Members' Bills is correct?
o: No body can allot time for such Bills in the Rajya Sabha
The Rajya Sabha's Business Advisory Committee allots time for Private Members' Bills
The Rajya Sabha has a Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions identical to the Lok Sabha committee
The President allots time for such Bills in the Rajya Sabha
x: The Rajya Sabha has no separate Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions for this purpose; its Business Advisory Committee allots the time.
tq: Distinguish the Lok Sabha committee from the Rajya Sabha's Business Advisory Committee.
sec: Private member's bills vs government bills

s: How many Private Members' Bills have become law, and in which year was the last such Bill enacted?
x: Only 14 Private Members' Bills have become law, and the last such enactment was in 1970.
tq: Pair the count with the year; do not treat the numerical figure and date as separate clues.
sec: Private member's bills vs government bills

s: Under Article 368 of the Constitution, a Constitutional Amendment Bill may be introduced in Parliament by
o: A Minister or a private member in either House
Only a Minister in either House
Only a private member in the Rajya Sabha
Only a Minister in the Lok Sabha
x: A Constitutional Amendment Bill under Article 368 may be introduced in either House by a Minister or a private member.
tq: Test who is legally authorised to introduce the Bill rather than assuming it is a government-only measure.
sec: Constitutional amendment bill - joint sitting, majority

s: Which one of the following is correct regarding the introduction of a Constitutional Amendment Bill under Article 368?
o: Prior recommendation of the President is not required
Prior recommendation of the President is compulsory
The Bill can be introduced only after ratification by half the States
Prior recommendation of the Governor is required
x: A Constitutional Amendment Bill does not require the President's prior recommendation for introduction. Ratification by half the States is required only for specified federal provisions after parliamentary passage.
tq: Use the prior-sanction distinction to separate Constitutional Amendment Bills from specified financial and territorial Bills.
sec: Constitutional amendment bill - joint sitting, majority

s:
With reference to a Constitutional Amendment Bill, consider the following statements:
1. A joint sitting may be summoned if the two Houses disagree.
2. The Bill fails if either House rejects it.
3. The President is constitutionally required to give assent after the Bill is duly passed.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: There is no provision for a joint sitting in respect of a Constitutional Amendment Bill; therefore, rejection by either House causes failure. Under the 24th Amendment, 1971, the President must give assent to a duly passed Constitutional Amendment Bill.
tq: Identify the constitutional exception to the ordinary deadlock procedure and the mandatory presidential assent.
sec: Constitutional amendment bill - joint sitting, majority

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched regarding Constitutional Amendment Bills and ordinary Bills?
o: Constitutional Amendment Bill — joint sitting possible in case of deadlock
Ordinary Bill — special majority in each House separately
Constitutional Amendment Bill — federal provisions may require ratification by half the States
Ordinary Bill — President must assent in every case
x: Certain Constitutional Amendments affecting federal provisions require ratification by at least half the States. Ordinary Bills generally require a simple majority, may be subject to joint sitting, and are not covered by mandatory assent in the same manner.
tq: Compare the deadlock, majority, ratification and assent columns before selecting the correctly matched pair.
sec: Constitutional amendment bill - joint sitting, majority

s: Which of the following provisions may be amended by a simple majority of Parliament and is consequently outside the procedure of Article 368?
o: Distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States
Representation of States in Parliament
Election of the President of India
Creation or abolition of a State Legislative Council
x: Creation or abolition of a State Legislative Council is provided for through a simple-majority procedure outside Article 368. The other subjects involve constitutional provisions requiring the Article 368 procedure, including possible State ratification.
tq: Look for the exceptional constitutional matters that are expressly outside Article 368.
sec: Constitutional amendment bill - joint sitting, majority

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Ratification by at least half of the States is required for every Constitutional Amendment.
2. For amendments affecting specified federal provisions, State ratification is required.
3. No time limit is prescribed for such State ratification.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: State ratification is not required for every Constitutional Amendment. It is required for specified federal provisions, and no time limit is prescribed for completing that ratification.
tq: Reject the absolute word “every” and retain the federal-provision exception.
sec: Constitutional amendment bill - joint sitting, majority

s: The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 was negatived in the Lok Sabha because it
o: was rejected by the Rajya Sabha after a joint sitting
was returned by the President for reconsideration
failed to secure a simple majority, receiving 230 votes in favour
secured 298 votes in favour but fell short of the special majority
x: The Bill received 298 votes in favour and 230 against out of 528 members present, but this was below the special majority required for a Constitutional Amendment Bill.
tq: Match the vote figures with the constitutional majority requirement and avoid confusing simple with special majority.
sec: Constitutional amendment bill - joint sitting, majority

s: The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 was associated with which of the following proposals?
o: Amendment of the procedure for passing Money Bills
Creation of a new State and abolition of its Legislative Council
Fast-track women's reservation and an increase in Lok Sabha strength from 550 to 850
Simultaneous elections through insertion of Article 82A
x: The 131st Amendment Bill, 2026 concerned fast-track women's reservation and proposed increasing Lok Sabha strength from 550 to 850.
tq: Separate the two contemporary amendment proposals by their subject matter and Article reference.
sec: Universal angles

s: The Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024, which was referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee, is associated with
o: One Nation, One Election and a proposed new Article 82A
The creation of Andhra State
The introduction of the annual financial statement
Fast-track women's reservation and 850 Lok Sabha seats
x: The 129th Amendment Bill, 2024 concerns simultaneous elections, or One Nation, One Election, and proposes a new Article 82A. It was referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee.
tq: Discriminate between the two numbered contemporary Constitutional Amendment Bills by their subject and proposed Article.
sec: Universal angles

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024:
1. It relates to simultaneous elections.
2. It proposes a new Article 82A.
3. It had already been enacted after receiving the required two-thirds majority in both Houses.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: The Bill relates to simultaneous elections and proposes Article 82A. It remained before the Joint Parliamentary Committee and had not been enacted after securing the required majority.
tq: Use the status trap: a Bill referred to a committee must not be treated as an enacted law.
sec: Universal angles

s: Which Article of the Constitution provides for the Annual Financial Statement?
o: Article 110
Article 114
Article 117
Article 112
x: Article 112 provides for the Annual Financial Statement, commonly called the Union Budget.
tq: Recall the article-to-provision pair directly from the financial provisions sequence.

Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
A. Article 112
B. Article 113
C. Article 114
D. Article 115

List-II (Provision)
1. Appropriation Bill
2. Supplementary, additional or excess grants
3. Annual Financial Statement
4. Procedure on estimates and demands for grants

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Article 112 concerns the Annual Financial Statement, Article 113 the procedure on estimates, Article 114 the Appropriation Bill, and Article 115 supplementary, additional or excess grants.
tq: Start with the secure Article 112–Budget pair and complete the consecutive financial-Article sequence.

s: The Union Budget is prepared by the Budget Division of the
o: Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance
Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance
Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance
Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs
x: The Budget is prepared by the Budget Division in the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance.
tq: Apply the “which department does this job?” authority-identification method.

s: The Annual Financial Statement of the Union is laid before Parliament by the
o: Union Finance Minister
Speaker of the Lok Sabha
Prime Minister
President
x: The Annual Financial Statement is laid before both Houses of Parliament by the President under the constitutional financial procedure.
tq: Distinguish the authority that formally lays the statement from the authority that prepares or presents it.

s: The first Union Budget of independent India was presented by R. K. Shanmukham Chetty on
o: 15 August 1947
26 November 1947
26 January 1950
1 February 2017
x: R. K. Shanmukham Chetty presented the first Union Budget of independent India on 26 November 1947.
tq: Use the date-person association rather than confusing the first Budget with later Budget-calendar changes.

s: Since 2017, the Union Budget has generally been presented on
o: 1 April
26 November
1 January
1 February
x: From 2017 onwards, the Union Budget has generally been presented on 1 February. The Budget for 2026–27 was presented on 1 February 2026.

s:
With reference to Demands for Grants, consider the following statements:
1. They are voted only by the Lok Sabha.
2. The Rajya Sabha may discuss them but cannot vote on them.
3. Charged expenditure is discussed but is not submitted to vote.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: All three statements are correct. Demands for Grants are voted by the Lok Sabha, while the Rajya Sabha can discuss them; charged expenditure is discussed but not voted upon.
tq: Separate voting power over demands from the power to discuss charged expenditure.
sec: Budget - Annual Financial Statement, Arts. 112-117, guillotine, cut motions, vote on account

s: In parliamentary financial procedure, the guillotine refers to
o: putting all outstanding demands to vote without discussion on the last day
the automatic rejection of all demands for grants
the President's power to withhold assent to a Money Bill
the referral of a financial Bill to a Joint Parliamentary Committee
x: On the last day fixed for the discussion of demands, all outstanding demands are put to vote without further discussion. This procedure is called the guillotine.
tq: Recognise the procedural meaning of a specialised parliamentary term.
sec: Budget - Annual Financial Statement, Arts. 112-117, guillotine, cut motions, vote on account

s:
Match the following types of cut motions with their purposes:

List-I (Cut motion)
A. Policy cut
B. Economy cut
C. Token cut

List-II (Purpose or amount)
1. Reduction by a specified amount to effect economy
2. Reduction of the demand to Re 1 to express disapproval of policy
3. Reduction by Rs 100 to ventilate a specific grievance

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: A policy cut reduces the demand to Re 1, an economy cut reduces it by a specified amount, and a token cut reduces it by Rs 100 to raise a specific grievance.
tq: Start from the distinctive numerical values—Re 1 and Rs 100—and then identify the remaining pair.
sec: Budget - Annual Financial Statement, Arts. 112-117, guillotine, cut motions, vote on account

s: A cut motion reducing a demand for grant to Re 1 signifies
o: a specific grievance against an individual minister
rejection of the entire Annual Financial Statement
disapproval of the policy underlying the demand
a demand for economy in expenditure
x: A policy cut motion proposes reducing the demand to Re 1 and expresses disapproval of the policy underlying the demand.
tq: Link the exact reduction amount with the purpose of the cut motion.
sec: Budget - Annual Financial Statement, Arts. 112-117, guillotine, cut motions, vote on account

s: Which of the following correctly describes a Vote on Account?
o: A vote by the Rajya Sabha on Demands for Grants
An advance grant for a part of the year until the Budget is passed
A permanent appropriation for the whole financial year
A grant available only for defence expenditure
x: A Vote on Account is an advance grant, usually for two months, to meet expenditure until the Budget is passed. It is provided under Article 116.
tq: Use the duration-and-purpose test to distinguish temporary authorisation from an annual appropriation.
sec: Budget - Annual Financial Statement, Arts. 112-117, guillotine, cut motions, vote on account

s:
Consider the following statements about a Vote on Account:
1. It is provided under Article 116.
2. It is usually granted for two months.
3. It becomes unnecessary in election years because the Budget is presented on 1 February.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: A Vote on Account is covered by Article 116 and is usually granted for two months. It continues to be used in election years; the change to a 1 February Budget date has not made it ineffectual.
tq: Spot the false causal conclusion in statement 3 while retaining the article and duration facts.

o: Rs 1 lakh crore

s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Formation of Andhra State
B. Introduction of the Andhra State Bill in Parliament
C. Assent to the Andhra State Bill
D. Presentation of the first Union Budget of independent India
o: D, B, C, A
B, D, C, A
D, C, B, A
B, C, D, A
x: The first Union Budget was presented on 26 November 1947, the Andhra State Bill was introduced on 10 August 1953, assent was given on 14 September 1953, and Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953.
tq: Fix the earliest dated event first, then order the three Andhra State milestones.

s: The Andhra State Bill was introduced in Parliament on
o: 10 August 1953
26 November 1947
1 October 1953
14 September 1953
x: The Andhra State Bill was introduced in Parliament on 10 August 1953.

sec: Universal angles

s: Which one of the following sequences correctly represents the dates connected with the Andhra State Bill and the formation of Andhra State?
o: Introduction—10 August 1953; assent—14 September 1953; formation—1 October 1953
Introduction—14 September 1953; assent—10 August 1953; formation—1 October 1953
Introduction—10 August 1953; assent—1 October 1953; formation—14 September 1953
Introduction—1 October 1953; assent—14 September 1953; formation—10 August 1953
x: The Bill was introduced on 10 August 1953, received assent on 14 September 1953, and Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953.
tq: Order the legislative process by introduction, assent and commencement rather than by memorising isolated dates.

s: The Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council, in relation to a Money Bill, can
o: make recommendations within fourteen days
refer it to a joint sitting within fourteen days
reject it within fourteen days
amend it finally within fourteen days
x: The Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council can only make recommendations on a Money Bill within fourteen days. It cannot reject or amend the Bill finally.
tq: Apply the special limitation on the Upper House of a State Legislature to a Money Bill.

s: Under Article 200, the Governor may exercise which of the following options in relation to a Bill?
o: Refer every Bill directly to the Supreme Court
Return every Bill, including a Money Bill, for reconsideration
Dissolve the Legislative Assembly whenever a Bill is rejected
Assent, withhold assent, return a non-Money Bill, or reserve it for the President
x: The Governor's options under Article 200 include assent, withholding assent, returning a non-Money Bill for reconsideration, and reserving a Bill for the President. A Money Bill cannot be returned for reconsideration in the same manner.
tq: Use the authority-and-exception method, especially the distinction between Money Bills and non-Money Bills.

s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes Articles 200 and 201?
o: Article 200 concerns the Governor's options on State Bills, while Article 201 concerns Bills reserved for the President
Article 200 concerns judicial review, while Article 201 concerns parliamentary privileges
Article 200 concerns Union Money Bills, while Article 201 concerns State Budgets
Both Articles exclusively regulate Constitutional Amendment Bills
x: Article 200 deals with the Governor's action on Bills passed by the State Legislature. Article 201 deals with Bills reserved for the consideration of the President.
tq: Compare the constitutional authority associated with each Article instead of confusing State and Union procedures.

s: The five-judge Bench's advisory opinion on the Presidential Reference held that courts
o: can prescribe fixed timelines for Governors and declare deemed assent
must approve every Bill within fourteen days
cannot fix such timelines or declare deemed assent
can replace the Governor's decision with their own assent
x: The advisory opinion stated that courts cannot fix timelines for Governors in this context or declare deemed assent. It addressed the issues raised by the earlier debate on gubernatorial assent.
tq: Identify the precise legal conclusion and reject the reversed-power alternatives.
